@@ -0,0 +1,125 @@
+---
+title: Configure Microsoft Entra Private Access sign-in every time
+description: Configure, test, and deploy sign-in every time for selected Microsoft Entra Private Access apps with one Conditional Access policy and an enforced pilot.
+ms.topic: how-to
+ms.date: 11/02/2026
+ms.custom: msecd-doc-authoring-1026
+ai-usage: ai-generated
+ms.author: alexpav
+# Customer intent: As an administrator, I want to configure and test sign-in every time for selected private applications so that I can deploy reauthentication with an appropriate scope.
+---
+
+# Configure sign-in every time for Microsoft Entra Private Access (preview)
+
+As an administrator, use Microsoft Entra Private Access sign-in every time (preview) to require reauthentication for selected sensitive private applications. Select applications, configure one Conditional Access policy, test enforcement with a pilot group, and expand deployment.
+
+Before you begin, review the prerequisites, including the Global Secure Access client for Windows, version 2.34.222 or later. Decide whether to exclude other platforms or block their access before you enable the policy.
+
+## Prerequisites
+
+- A configured Global Secure Access Private Access setup, using [Quick Access](how-to-configure-quick-access.md) or [per-app access](how-to-configure-per-app-access.md).
+- A [Microsoft Entra Private Access license](overview-what-is-global-secure-access.md#licensing-overview).
+- The [Global Secure Access client for Windows](how-to-install-windows-client.md), version **2.34.222 or later**, on supported pilot devices.
+- At least the [Conditional Access Administrator](~/identity/role-based-access-control/permissions-reference.md#conditional-access-administrator) role to create and manage the policy.
+
+## Select applications and pilot users
+
+Start with specific higher-risk applications rather than all private applications. Choose applications where reauthentication adds protection and where the additional authentication prompts are appropriate for the users' work.
+
+Sign-in every time works with both Quick Access and per-app access. We recommend per-app targeting to avoid unexpected prompts for other resources included in a broad Quick Access configuration. For example, a Windows device joined to an on-premises domain opens a new network connection when it checks in with its domain controller. This connection might trigger an authentication prompt without an explicit user action to explain it. Setting up sign-in every time for specific per-app resources helps avoid these unexpected prompts.
+
+As a deployment best practice, we also recommend following [Manage emergency access accounts in Microsoft Entra ID](~/identity/role-based-access-control/security-emergency-access.md). Your emergency access accounts should be excluded from the sign-in every time policies.
+
+1. Work with application owners to identify the applications that need sign-in every time. For example:
+
+    | Application | Example use |
+    | --- | --- |
+    | Administrator jump box. | System administrators connect through SSH or RDP to manage sensitive infrastructure. |
+    | Financial system. | Staff submit or approve payments or other financial transactions. |
+    | Healthcare system. | Authorized staff access patient records or other sensitive clinical data. |
+
+1. Confirm that the five-minute Global Secure Access reauthentication window meets each application's requirements. This feature is triggered when a new network connection is established to the protected private application. It doesn't guarantee a fresh prompt for every command, transaction, or patient record. For the timing example, see [Reauthentication interval](concept-private-access-sign-in-every-time.md#reauthentication-interval).
+1. Identify the corresponding Private Access enterprise applications. If the resources are part of a broad Quick Access configuration, consider [per-app access segmentation](tutorial-private-access-app-segmentation.md) to target them individually.
+1. Select a small pilot group that represents the applications and client platforms you plan to support. Confirm that pilot users already have the required application assignments; Conditional Access user targeting doesn't grant application access.
+1. Record the selected applications, pilot group, planned user scope, and exclusions. Keep existing Conditional Access protections in place.
+
+Use one Conditional Access policy for the selected applications that share this sign-in every time requirement and user scope. The feature doesn't have an application-specific interval to configure: select **Every time strict (preview)** and add relevant applications to the same policy as needed.
+
+## Choose the platform scope
+
+Decide how to handle unsupported platforms before enforcement. The choice determines whether those users can connect without this policy's sign-in every time protection or are blocked.
+
+1. Choose one of these approaches:
+
+    | Approach | Policy scope | Expected behavior |
+    | --- | --- | --- |
+    | Enforce only on Windows. | Use the **Device platforms** condition to include Windows and leave non-Windows platforms out of scope. | Supported Windows clients use sign-in every time. Other platforms aren't subject to this policy and can connect if their other access requirements are satisfied. |
+    | Require enforcement across targeted platforms. | Don't exclude platforms from the policy. | Supported Windows clients use sign-in every time. Global Secure Access blocks access from unsupported platforms or older Windows clients where enforcement applies. |
+
+1. Check Windows client versions for users in scope. Windows-only targeting doesn't distinguish client versions: Windows clients earlier than **2.34.222** are still blocked where enforcement applies.
+1. Agree on the platform choice with application owners and communicate expected prompts or blocked access to pilot users.
+
+For more information, see [Supported clients and platforms](concept-private-access-sign-in-every-time.md#supported-clients-and-platforms) and [Conditional Access device platform conditions](~/identity/conditional-access/concept-conditional-access-conditions.md#device-platforms).
+
+## Create one Conditional Access policy
+
+Create the policy in the **Off** state so you can review its scope before enabling the pilot:
+
+> [!WARNING]
+> Don't apply **Every time strict (preview)** to Office 365 applications or broadly to all resources.
+
+1. Sign in to the [Microsoft Entra admin center](https://entra.microsoft.com) as at least a **Conditional Access Administrator**.
+1. Browse to **Entra ID** > **Conditional Access** > **Policies** and select **New policy**.
+1. Enter a descriptive name, such as **Private Access - Sign-in every time**.
+1. Under **Assignments** > **Users**, include your selected pilot users or group.
+1. Under **Users** > **Exclude**, configure your intended user or group exclusions. If you use emergency access accounts, we recommend excluding them or their dedicated group, following the [current emergency access guidance](~/identity/role-based-access-control/security-emergency-access.md#conditional-access-considerations).
+1. Under **Target resources** > **Resources (formerly cloud apps)** > **Include**, choose **Select resources** and select the Private Access enterprise applications identified earlier.
+1. Under **Conditions** > **Device platforms**, apply your platform decision:
+
+    - For Windows-only enforcement, set **Configure** to **Yes**, choose **Select device platforms** under **Include**, and select **Windows**.
+    - For enforcement across targeted platforms, leave the device platform condition unconfigured so it doesn't remove unsupported platforms from scope.
+
+1. Under **Access controls** > **Session**, select **Sign-in frequency**, choose **Every time strict (preview)**, and select **Select**.
+1. Set **Enable policy** to **Off** and select **Create**.
+1. Review the saved policy's applications, pilot users, platform condition, and exclusions before enabling it.
+
+> [!IMPORTANT]
+> Select **Every time strict (preview)**. The **Every time** option does not apply to Global Secure Access private applications.
+
+## Test with an enforced pilot
+
+Enable the policy only for the selected pilot users and applications. Test actual access and prompts before expanding the policy.
+
+1. Review your intended exclusions and verify that your recovery process works. If you use emergency access accounts, confirm that they're excluded as recommended. Notify pilot users and application owners before enforcement.
+1. Open the saved policy, set **Enable policy** to **On**, and select **Save**.
+1. Use a Windows pilot device with Global Secure Access client **2.34.222 or later**. Wait more than five minutes after the last sign-in to a selected private application, then connect to that application. Complete reauthentication and record the time.
+1. Close the application connection. You need to ensure that the application process which initiated the connection is completely closed (this ensures that the network flow is terminated). Reconnect less than five minutes after that authentication and confirm that sign-in every time doesn't trigger another prompt.
+1. Close the connection again, again ensuring that the application process exits. Reconnect more than five minutes after the recorded authentication and confirm that reauthentication is required.
+1. Repeat the test for the selected applications and representative users. Confirm that users can complete their work after reauthentication.
+1. Test the scope and compatibility cases in the following table.
+
+    | Test case | Expected result from this policy |
+    | --- | --- |
+    | A targeted Windows user has a client earlier than 2.34.222. | Access is blocked where sign-in every time is enforced. |
+    | A non-Windows platform is in scope. | Access is blocked because the platform doesn't support this feature. |
+    | A non-Windows platform is outside scope under the Windows-only approach. | This policy doesn't enforce sign-in every time. Other policies and access requirements still apply. |
+    | A user is excluded, or an application isn't targeted. | This policy doesn't enforce sign-in every time for that access. Other policies and access requirements still apply. |
+
+1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, browse to **Entra ID** > **Monitoring & health** > **Sign-in logs**. Find the pilot sign-ins and review their **Conditional Access** details. Confirm the expected policy applies or is out of scope, and compare the results with access and prompts observed on the client.
+
+For help investigating policy results, see [Troubleshoot Conditional Access](~/identity/conditional-access/troubleshoot-conditional-access.md). If an expected test fails, resolve it before expanding deployment.
+
+## Expand deployment and monitor
+
+Expand the same policy only after the enforced pilot meets the application's requirements. Review client readiness and exclusions for each expansion.
+
+1. Add approved user groups to the policy in stages, retaining any configured emergency access exclusions. Notify each group about reauthentication and supported clients.
+1. Add further selected Private Access applications under **Target resources** in the same policy as needed. Confirm that the policy's user and platform scope is appropriate for each addition, and repeat the pilot tests.
+1. Monitor sign-in results, unexpected access failures, and user feedback. Check that platform exclusions remain consistent with the access requirements agreed with application owners.
+1. If enforcement causes unexpected disruption, open the sign-in every time policy and set **Enable policy** to **Off**, then select **Save**. Alternatively, reduce its scope to the validated pilot users and applications. Leave other security policies in place and verify recovery before retrying rollout.
+
+## Related content
+
+- [Microsoft Entra Private Access sign-in every time overview](concept-private-access-sign-in-every-time.md).
+- [Apply Conditional Access policies to Private Access apps](how-to-target-resource-private-access-apps.md).
+- [Plan a Conditional Access deployment](~/identity/conditional-access/plan-conditional-access.md).

+### Getting Permission Denied when trying to connect to a Red Hat Enterprise Linux VM after performing an in-place upgrade from RHEL 8.x to RHEL 9.x
+
+After an in-place upgrade of the VM from RHEL 8.x to RHEL 9.x, a Microsoft Entra ID SSH sign-in might fail with `Permission denied (publickey)` If the VM was configured for Microsoft Entra login before the upgrade.
+
+This issue happens as the package `aadsshlogin` may be removed automatically during the upgrade process because Leapp treats that as a third-party package.
+
+> [!NOTE]
+>Third-party packages may be removed automatically during the upgrade if they depend on official distribution content which is not present on the target system - therefore RPM dependencies of such packages cannot be satisfied and hence such packages cannot be installed on the target system. 
+For more information, see [Handling the migration of your custom and third-party applications](https://red.ht/customize-rhel-upgrade-actors)
+
+Workaround:
+
+The solution is to uninstall the AADLoginForLinux VM extension from the VM, and then reinstall it again.
+
+1. Uninstall the AADLoginForLinux extension on the VM:
+
+```azurecli-interactive
+az vm extension delete -g MyResourceGroup --vm-name MyVm -n AADSSHLoginForLinux
+```
+
+1. Install the AADSSHLoginForLinux extension on the VM:
+	
+```azurecli-interactive
+az vm extension set --publisher Microsoft.Azure.ActiveDirectory --name AADSSHLoginForLinux --resource-group myResourceGroup --vm-name myVM
+```
+

+### Every time strict (preview)
+
+**Every time strict (preview)** is a sign-in frequency control with a shorter validity window (10 seconds) for authentication freshness. Examples include pharmaceutical e-prescribing applications and financial or banking applications that require reauthentication for sensitive actions.
+
+To require fresh authentication for a sensitive action, an application needs compatible session management. That logic must request a new token for the action. Applying the control alone isn't sufficient if the application continues to use its existing session without requesting a new token.

messageCenterItems.title: Microsoft Entra ID: Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication to retire for self-service password reset (SSPR)
messageCenterItems.summary: Microsoft Entra ID will retire Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication for self-service password reset (SSPR) starting February 2027, with a 50-day transition per user group. Organizations must prepare alternative recovery methods, as SMS/voice will no longer be available for SSPR after the transition.
messageCenterItems.body:
What and why

As Microsoft-provided SMS and voice authentication retire in Microsoft Entra ID, these methods will also become unavailable for SSPR. Organizations have 50 days after the applicable sign-in retirement rollout reaches their tenant to prepare alternative recovery methods. Users may still be able to sign in but lose the ability to reset forgotten passwords. Passkeys and other sign-in methods don't automatically satisfy SSPR requirements. Admins should identify affected users and ensure they have enough eligible recovery methods to prevent disruptions and increased helpdesk requests.

Rollout schedule

  • General Availability (Worldwide, GCC): We expect rollout to begin and complete in February 2027

User populationSign-in retirement rollout beginsSSPR transition ends
Users other than Global Administrators and external usersFebruary 1, 202750 days after this rollout reaches your tenant
Global Administrators and external usersJuly 1, 202750 days after this separate rollout reaches your tenant

These are phased rollout start dates, not a single SSPR cutoff for every organization. Each population's 50-day period begins when its applicable rollout reaches your tenant. 

Impact on your organization

Who is affected

  • Organizations with users who rely on Microsoft-provided SMS/voice to meet their password-reset verification requirements. This includes users who have another sign-in method but still depend on SMS/voice for password recovery.

Platforms and services

  • Microsoft Entra ID SSPR

What will happen

When the applicable sign-in retirement rollout reaches your tenant:

  • 50-day transition: Existing SMS and voice registrations remain usable for SSPR under your current recovery policy.
  • Registration changes: SMS/voice SSPR registration and refresh prompts stop, but prompts for other eligible methods continue.
  • My Sign-Ins: Users can no longer add SMS/voice methods or edit authentication phone numbers. Existing phone registrations appear disabled, even while usable for SSPR during the transition.
  • Customer-managed telephony (CYOT): Recovery through supported providers remains available.

After the 50-day transition period:

Microsoft-provided SMS and voice are no longer available as SSPR recovery options.

User's remaining eligible recovery methodsPassword-reset experience
Enough methods to meet the applicable SSPR requirementUser can continue resetting their password with those methods
Not enough methods to meet the applicable SSPR requirementUser cannot complete SSPR and is directed to contact their administrator

The applicable one/two method requirement still applies. To retain SMS/voice for recovery, your organization must configure a supported CYOT.

Microsoft will not automatically change your SSPR policy or enable Allow password change after secure sign-in for your tenant.

Action required and recommendations

Prepare affected users before their applicable 50-day transition period ends:

  1. Identify affected users. Find users relying on SMS/voice for SSPR, even if they have other sign-in methods registered. Use the SMS and voice retirement and migration guidance.
  2. Prepare alternative recovery methods. Ensure users have enough eligible methods to meet SSPR policy requirements without Microsoft-provided SMS/voice. Passkeys alone don't satisfy SSPR requirements. If phone recovery is needed, configure and test a supported telephony provider before the transition ends.
  3. Test and communicate. Verify password recovery works with your SSPR policies and Conditional Access settings. Inform users and helpdesk staff about deadlines, registration steps, and support options.

Recommended: Let passkey users change a forgotten password

  • Where available, administrators can enable Allow password change after secure sign-in for eligible users. Users can then sign in with their passkey and change their password in My Sign-Ins without knowing/entering their current password.

Learn more

  • SMS and voice retirement and migration guidance
  • How Microsoft Entra self-service password reset works
  • Choose a telephony provider for SMS and voice authentication

Compliance considerations

If your organization needs phone-based recovery for regulatory or operational reasons, plan and validate a supported customer-managed provider before the applicable SSPR cutoff.

messageCenterItems.title: Microsoft Defender for Office 365: Changes to Unified RBAC permission mapping for Microsoft Entra Security Operator role
messageCenterItems.summary: Microsoft is updating the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Unified RBAC mapping for the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role, removing default access to email threat policies and Tenant Allow/Block List. Rollout starts December 2026. Organizations must manually assign permissions if continued access is needed.
messageCenterItems.body:
Updated November 3, 2026: We have updated the timeline. Thank you for your patience. 

What and why

We are updating the Microsoft Defender unified role-based access control (Unified RBAC) permission mapping for Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (Email & Collaboration). Currently, the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role includes the Authorization and settings\Security settings permission through the default Unified RBAC mapping. As a result, users assigned this role can view and manage email threat policies and the Tenant Allow/Block List.

To align access with documented Microsoft Defender for Office 365 role expectations and least-privilege principles, we are updating the default mapping so that Authorization and settings\Security settings (All permissions) is no longer included by default for the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role mapping for the Microsoft Defender for Office 365 workload. After this change, organizations that have Unified RBAC enabled and rely only on the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role for this access will need to manually assign the appropriate permissions or assign a role that includes those permissions.

Rollout schedule

  • General Availability (Worldwide, GCC, GCC High, DoD): Rollout begins in early December 2026 (previously early November) and is expected to complete by mid-January 2027 (previously early December 2026).

Impact on your organization

Who is affected

  • Organizations where both of the following conditions apply:
    1. Microsoft Defender XDR Unified RBAC is enabled, or will be enabled, for Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (Email & Collaboration).
    2. Users assigned the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role.

Platforms and services

  • Microsoft Defender for Office 365 (Email & Collaboration)
  • Microsoft Defender XDR Unified RBAC
  • Microsoft Entra ID

What will happen

  • The default Unified RBAC mapping for the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role will be updated to align with its documented Microsoft Defender for Office 365 scope and least-privilege principles.
  • When Unified RBAC is enabled for Microsoft Defender for Office 365, by default, the Security Operator role will no longer provide access to view, create, edit, or delete email threat policies, including anti-spam, anti-phishing, anti-malware, Safe Links, Safe Attachments, and preset security policies. The role will also no longer provide access to view, add, edit, or remove Tenant Allow/Block List entries.
  • This change applies only to Microsoft Defender for Office 365 when Unified RBAC is enabled. Tenants that have not enabled Unified RBAC are not affected.
  • Organizations that want operators to retain access can manually assign the appropriate Unified RBAC permissions, including Core security settings and Detection tuning, or assign a role that already includes those permissions, such as Security Administrator.
  • Other role mappings and existing Exchange Online PowerShell authorization are unchanged.

Action required and recommendations

We recommend that you:

  • Review users who are assigned the Microsoft Entra Security Operator role and determine whether they rely on that role to view or manage email threat policies or the Tenant Allow/Block List.
  • If continued access is required, assign an appropriate role or grant the required Unified RBAC permissions, including Core security settings and Detection tuning.
  • Update internal operational procedures, runbooks, and access-control documentation as needed.
  • Communicate this change to security operations teams and help desk staff.

Learn more

  • Activate Microsoft Defender unified role-based access control (URBAC) - Microsoft Defender XDR | Microsoft Learn
  • Create custom roles with Microsoft Defender unified role-based access control (RBAC) - Microsoft Defender XDR | Microsoft Learn
  • Map Microsoft Defender unified role-based access control (RBAC) permissions - Microsoft Defender XDR | Microsoft Learn
  • Permissions in Microsoft Defender unified role-based access control (RBAC) - Microsoft Defender XDR | Microsoft Learn

Compliance considerations

No compliance considerations identified. Review as appropriate for your organization.

highlights.headline: identity/conditional-access
highlights.detail: The documentation now states that Office perpetual clients version 2024 and later support Token Protection, while versions earlier than 2024 aren't supported. The documentation now describes Every time strict, including its 10-second validity window, application session-management requirements, targeting guidance, and Office 365 warning. It also explains Global Secure Access reauthentication for sensitive private applications using a five-minute window.

highlights.headline: identity/hybrid
highlights.detail: The guide now covers connecting with Microsoft Graph PowerShell, required permissions and cloud settings, troubleshooting consent, and the PowerShell command for changing a group’s source of authority. The documentation now explains how to install and connect with Microsoft Graph PowerShell, select cloud environments, grant required permissions, and update a user’s source of authority with PowerShell. The Update-MgGroupOnPremiseSyncBehavior and Get-MgGroupOnPremiseSyncBehavior links no longer include the graph-powershell-1.0 view parameter. The User Source of Authority configuration guide now links to the current Microsoft Graph PowerShell cmdlet pages without the `view=graph-powershell-1.0`

highlights.headline: identity/authentication
highlights.detail: The documentation now directs administrators through Function App → Functions → SendOtp → Invocations when checking the latest transaction and HTTP 200 result. The table now lists External multifactor authentication as method 3, Certificate-based authentication as method 4, and Microsoft Authenticator notifications as method 5. The External MFA entry also has updated dash formatting.

highlights.headline: external-id
highlights.detail: The documentation now describes the sample as supporting passkey listing, registration, and deletion. It removes the separate deletion endpoint guidance and the warning about the sample using Microsoft Graph with high-privilege permissions and a client secret.

highlights.headline: identity-platform
highlights.detail: The article now says the passkey sample demonstrates listing, registration, and deletion flows, and removes the previous Microsoft Graph deletion-flow warning.

highlights.headline: identity/saas-apps
highlights.detail: The tutorial now requires SOAP API `login()` to be enabled and the Admin Username account to have **Use Any API Auth**. It also documents credential-validation troubleshooting and Salesforce’s December 1, 2026 requirement. The tutorial adds requirements to enable SOAP API `login()` and grant the integration account API Enabled, Manage Users, and Use Any API Auth permissions. It also documents Salesforce’s December 1, 2026 requirement for Use Any API Auth and related credential errors.

highlights.headline: identity/app-provisioning
highlights.detail: The account discovery preview documentation now explains how to view discovered groups’ member counts and membership lists.
